FIELDNOTES / Data & AI A practitioner’s perspective
A PERSPECTIVE BY RAJAT VERMA

Building the foundations
for useful AI.

Reliable data. Shared meaning. Relevant context.
How they come together to help agents do useful work.

Data & AI Fieldnotes/November 1, 2026Explore the references ↓

My view is that enterprise AI is as much a data-product challenge as a model challenge. An agent needs evidence it can trust, a consistent understanding of the business, and enough context to judge what matters for the task in front of it.

I think about that foundation as three connected responsibilities: making data dependable, making meaning reusable, and making context relevant. The value appears when an agent can use all three to produce a result someone can inspect and act on.

01 / DATA

Start with evidence people can trust.

A good data layer makes records discoverable, timely, and dependable. That means clear ownership, understood grain, tested transformations, lineage, and access controls. A table’s existence says little about whether it is fit for a particular decision.

For an agent, a successful query can still return the wrong population or incomplete data. I want freshness, coverage, and known limitations to be visible alongside the values. These are part of the product’s usefulness.

02 / SEMANTICS

Turn business meaning into a shared contract.

Data supports a semantic layer when teams explicitly model what it means: entities, relationships, metrics, dimensions, and the rules for calculating them. “Active customer” needs an agreed population, qualifying activity, and time window. Those definitions should be owned, versioned, and testable.

The payoff is reuse: dashboards, analysts, and agents can work from the same definition. I would standardize recurring, consequential questions first, while leaving room to explore new ones. Shared semantics should make interpretation more consistent without freezing analytical work.

One implementation: Netflix’s DataJunction connects metric definitions in a semantic graph and serves them through APIs.

03 / CONTEXT

Bring the right meaning to the current task.

A semantic layer is one input to a broader context layer. Here, I use “context layer” to mean the system that assembles relevant definitions, documentation, examples, lineage, current state, and user intent for a particular task. These responsibilities can span several tools.

A metric may be correctly defined and still be inappropriate for the question. The agent may need to know about a launch, an ingestion delay, or a business-unit exception. Useful context should carry its source and scope, stay current, and surface disagreement. More retrieved text is not automatically better guidance.

OpenAI’s internal data agent combines table knowledge, human annotations, institutional knowledge, memory, and live context. Read the engineering account ↗

AN ILLUSTRATIVE EXAMPLE

“Why did retention fall this month?”

Data
Are the customer events complete, and has the latest period finished loading?
Semantics
Which retention definition, cohort, and time window should apply?
Context
Did a launch, tracking change, or segment shift affect the comparison?
Agent
Clarify ambiguity, compare appropriate cohorts, inspect evidence, and distinguish a possible explanation from a demonstrated cause.

A useful response makes the definition, evidence, and uncertainty visible. Any follow-up action has its own permission and approval requirements.

04 / INTELLIGENCE

Make intelligence an operating capability.

These foundations give a model something dependable to reason over. Useful execution also requires well-defined tools, checks on intermediate results, and workflows that can recover from failure. Permissions must be enforced by the systems executing queries and actions; instructions in a prompt are insufficient.

For practitioners, I would prioritize the ability to trace a failure to its source: bad data, missing semantics, stale context, or incorrect agent behavior. That diagnosis should lead to a testable change. Corrections need review before they become shared knowledge, and production workflows need monitoring and safe recovery.

My product test is whether people can complete useful work with less verification and repair. I would measure task success, correctness, time to a verified result, and operating cost together. A fluent response is only the beginning.

WHERE I LAND

The foundation is a product in its own right: something practitioners can build, inspect, improve, and reuse—and something people can trust when an agent puts it to work.

This is my synthesis of the ideas explored here. The references below offer implementations, tradeoffs, and counterpoints; they do not all share the same architecture or conclusions.
